papers.title: TOEFL iBT (2026 format): Practice Test 1
papers.intro: Follows the task types of the TOEFL iBT introduced on 21 January 2026: Reading (Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life, Read an Academic Passage), Listening (Choose a Response, Conversation, Announcement, Academic Talk), Writing (Build a Sentence, Write an Email, Academic Discussion) and Speaking (Listen and Repeat, Take an Interview). The real test is adaptive; this practice version is fixed. Scores are estimated on the 1–6 band scale.

parts.title: Read an Academic Passage
parts.passage:
The domestication of plants did not happen in a single place or at a single moment. Archaeological evidence indicates that agriculture emerged independently in at least a dozen regions, including the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and parts of Africa, over a period of several thousand years. In each case, people gradually began to favour plants with useful traits, such as seeds that remained on the stalk instead of scattering, which made harvesting easier.

For a long time, scholars assumed that farming spread because it obviously improved human life. Skeletal remains complicate this picture. Early farming populations often show signs of poorer nutrition and more dental disease than the hunter-gatherers who preceded them, probably because their diets relied heavily on a few starchy crops. Why, then, did agriculture spread? One explanation is demographic: farming produces more food per area of land, even if that food is less varied, allowing populations to grow. Once a community had committed to farming and its numbers had increased, returning to hunting and gathering was no longer a realistic option.

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about where agriculture began?
options: It began in the Fertile Crescent and spread everywhere.
It emerged independently in many regions.
questions.answer: It emerged independently in many regions.
questions.explanation: 'independently in at least a dozen regions'.

questions.prompt: Why were seeds that stayed on the stalk useful?
questions.answer: They made harvesting easier.

questions.prompt: What do skeletal remains of early farmers often show?
options: Poorer nutrition and more dental disease.
questions.answer: Poorer nutrition and more dental disease.

questions.prompt: The word 'complicate' in paragraph 2 suggests that the skeletal evidence…
options: makes the old assumption harder to accept.
questions.answer: makes the old assumption harder to accept.
questions.explanation: It challenges the idea that farming obviously improved life.

questions.prompt: According to the demographic explanation, why did farming persist?
options: Larger populations could not return to hunting and gathering.
questions.answer: Larger populations could not return to hunting and gathering.

lines.t: Today let's look at a puzzle in economics known as the paradox of thrift.
For an individual household, saving more is usually sensible. But if everyone tries to save more at the same time, total spending in the economy falls.
Lower spending means lower sales for businesses, which may respond by cutting jobs. As incomes fall, households may end up saving no more than before, or even less.
The idea is closely associated with John Maynard Keynes, who used it to argue that governments should increase spending during recessions.
Not all economists accept the paradox. Some argue that higher savings lower interest rates, which encourages investment and offsets the fall in consumption.

questions.prompt: What is the paradox of thrift?
options: If everyone saves more at once, total saving may not rise.
questions.answer: If everyone saves more at once, total saving may not rise.

questions.prompt: How might businesses respond to lower spending?
questions.answer: By cutting jobs.

questions.prompt: What policy did Keynes support based on this idea?
questions.answer: Increased government spending in recessions.

questions.prompt: What counter-argument does the professor mention?
options: Higher savings lower interest rates and encourage investment.
questions.answer: Higher savings lower interest rates and encourage investment.

parts.title: Part 5: Multiple-choice reading
parts.passage:
When I first started working as a translator, I believed that my job was to be invisible. A good translation, I had been told, should read as though it had been written in the target language, without any trace of the original. I spent hours searching for idiomatic equivalents, smoothing out awkward phrases and removing anything that might strike an English reader as foreign.

It was a novel by a Brazilian writer that changed my mind. The author's sentences were long and winding, full of repetitions that, in Portuguese, created a hypnotic rhythm. My first draft was fluent and readable — and, I realised with some discomfort, rather dull. In making the book sound English, I had removed precisely what made it distinctive.

The author, whom I eventually met at a literary festival, was surprisingly relaxed about the question. 'Every translation is a new book,' she told me. 'I only ask that it be a good one.' It was generous of her, but it did not quite resolve my dilemma. A translator who departs too freely from the original risks imposing their own voice; one who follows it too closely produces something unreadable.

I now think of translation less as a search for the right answer than as a series of negotiated compromises. I keep some of the strangeness, enough to remind readers that the book comes from elsewhere, while making sure that it never becomes an obstacle. Whether I strike the right balance is, inevitably, a matter of opinion. But I no longer aim to be invisible.

options: It should preserve the original's foreign feel.
It should read as if originally written in the target language.

questions.answer: It should read as if originally written in the target language.

questions.answer: It had lost what made the book distinctive.
questions.explanation: 'I had removed precisely what made it distinctive.'

It made the writer stop translating.
questions.answer: It was kind but did not fully settle the writer's dilemma.
questions.explanation: 'generous… but it did not quite resolve my dilemma'.

parts.title: Multiple choice: Interview with a museum curator

lines.t: My guest today is a museum curator who has just reopened a gallery after a two-year renovation. What was the thinking behind the changes?

Honestly, our visitor surveys told us that people found the old layout exhausting. Hundreds of objects, tiny labels, no clear story. We were showing everything we owned rather than explaining anything.
So you've reduced the number of objects?

By about a third. Some colleagues were uneasy about that; it can feel like hiding the collection. But everything we removed is now available to researchers by appointment, and much of it has been photographed for our online catalogue.
And what has the public reaction been?

Visitors are staying longer, which surprised us, given there's less to see. I think when people aren't overwhelmed, they actually look. The one complaint we've had is about the lighting, which some people find too dim. That's deliberate, to protect fragile textiles, but we're adding better signage to explain why.

questions.prompt: Why was the gallery redesigned?
options: Visitors found the old layout overwhelming.
The museum had too few objects.
questions.answer: Visitors found the old layout overwhelming.

questions.prompt: How does the curator respond to concerns about 'hiding the collection'?
options: Removed objects can still be seen by researchers and online.
The objects were put in storage permanently.
questions.answer: Removed objects can still be seen by researchers and online.

questions.prompt: What surprised the museum after reopening?
options: Visitors stayed longer despite seeing fewer objects.
questions.answer: Visitors stayed longer despite seeing fewer objects.

questions.prompt: What is the curator's response to complaints about lighting?

The dim lighting will stay, but signs will explain why.
questions.answer: The dim lighting will stay, but signs will explain why.

parts.title: Part 5: Multiple-choice reading
parts.passage:
There is a particular kind of silence that descends on a concert hall in the moments before the music begins — not the absence of sound, exactly, but a collective holding of breath. I have spent much of my career trying to understand what happens in that silence, and I am no closer to an answer than when I began.

The conventional explanation is that the audience is simply waiting, and that the silence is a courtesy, a clearing of space. But that strikes me as too modest. The silence is not merely the frame around the performance; it is part of it. Anyone who has heard a great conductor wait, seemingly interminably, before the first note knows that the tension generated in those seconds shapes everything that follows.

This is, I suspect, why recordings, for all their technical perfection, so often disappoint. They begin, as it were, mid-sentence. The silence that precedes them is the silence of a living room or a car, a silence that belongs to the listener alone and therefore carries no shared expectation. We have gained the ability to hear any music at any time, and lost, without quite noticing, the communal anticipation that once gave it weight.

I do not wish to romanticise the concert hall. It is an institution with its own absurdities, from the ritual coughing between movements to the anxious etiquette of applause. Nor am I suggesting that we abandon recorded music, which has brought extraordinary works to millions who would otherwise never have heard them. My point is narrower: that something is lost when music becomes a commodity always within reach, and that what is lost is precisely what cannot be recorded.

options: As an integral part of the performance.
questions.answer: As an integral part of the performance.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the writer, do recordings often disappoint?
options: They lack the shared anticipation that precedes live music.
questions.answer: They lack the shared anticipation that precedes live music.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To qualify the argument and avoid overstatement.
questions.answer: To qualify the argument and avoid overstatement.
questions.explanation: 'I do not wish to romanticise… My point is narrower'.

lack a meaningful lead-in of shared silence.
questions.answer: lack a meaningful lead-in of shared silence.
questions.explanation: Metaphor for the missing communal silence.

tasks.label: Essay (240–280 words)
tasks.prompt:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The value of failure: Educational systems that punish every mistake teach students to avoid risk. Yet it is through failure that we learn most deeply: an error forces us to reconsider our assumptions in a way that success never does. Schools should therefore create spaces where experimentation is rewarded even when it does not succeed.

Text 2 — The limits of failure: The fashionable celebration of failure ignores an uncomfortable truth: not everyone can afford to fail. For students from disadvantaged backgrounds, a single poor result can close doors permanently. Encouraging risk-taking without providing a safety net merely transfers the cost of experimentation onto those least able to bear it.

parts.title: Multiple choice: Discussion about urban planning

lines.t: There's been a great deal of enthusiasm recently for the so-called fifteen-minute city, where daily needs are within a short walk or cycle. You've been rather more cautious.
Cautious, yes, but not opposed. The principle is sound: fewer car journeys, livelier neighbourhoods. My reservation is that it's often presented as a design problem, when it's really an economic one.
In what sense?

You can zone a street for shops, but you can't make a shop viable. Local businesses need enough customers within that radius, which means a certain density of population. Many suburbs simply don't have it, and no amount of clever planning will conjure it up.
So is the idea doomed outside dense city centres?

Not doomed, but it has to be pursued gradually and honestly. The danger is that the label becomes a marketing exercise, attached to developments that are, in practice, as car-dependent as ever. That breeds cynicism, and cynicism is very hard to undo.

questions.answer: Supportive in principle but cautious.

options: Local shops need enough nearby customers to survive.
questions.answer: Local shops need enough nearby customers to survive.

questions.prompt: What danger does the planner warn about?
options: The label being used as marketing for car-dependent developments.
questions.answer: The label being used as marketing for car-dependent developments.
